title: PMS Distributor
blurb: Portfolio Management Services: suitability, due diligence, fees and behaviour for high-ticket clients.

rows: New employees (all sections), sales team (talk-tracks, role-plays, niche topics)
One 75–90 minute session, plus 20 minutes of role-play and the quiz
Module 1 (MF Distributors); the required PMS distributor certification and registration before dealing with PMS clients
Each L.E.A.R.N. stage has: what to know, how to do it, a talk-track, and the investor takeaway
outcomes: Explain what a PMS is, how it differs from mutual funds and AIFs, and who it suits.
Judge suitability before recommending any PMS strategy.
Run due diligence on a strategy and explain its full fee structure with a worked example.
Review a PMS on after-fee returns against its benchmark.
Keep a client steady through the sharper falls that concentrated portfolios bring.

sources: Business Standard: SEBI puts expense cap on PMS providers (Feb 2020): ₹50 lakh minimum, exit-load caps, 0.5% expense cap, direct onboarding, net-of-fee reporting
Business Standard: SEBI performance benchmarking for PMS (Dec 2022): four strategies, APMI benchmarks, effective April 2023
Cafemutual: commission withheld without APRN: APRN deadlines and the 31 July 2025 cut-off
APMI: NISM XXI-A PMS Distributors Certificate Examination
Cafemutual: upfront commission allowed only till 30 June 2020

lessons.title: PMS vs mutual fund vs AIF
Who a PMS distributor is: NISM XXI-A, APRN and EUIN
Eligible is not the same as suitable
PMS fee structures, with a worked example

cards.q: What is the single most important idea in the PMS module?
a: Eligible is not the same as suitable. ₹50 lakh opens the door to PMS; our job is to decide, honestly, whether the client should walk through it.

cards.q: What is a PMS distributor's job, in order of priority?
a: Due diligence and suitability first, access second. PMS is a concentrated, high-ticket product held in the client's own name.

cards.q: What is a PMS?
a: A professionally managed portfolio of securities held directly in the client's own demat account, regulated by SEBI.

cards.q: The three numbers to remember about PMS?
a: ₹50 lakh: SEBI minimum investment
15–30 stocks: typical, concentrated portfolio
1 demat account in the client's own name

cards.q: What are the three types of PMS?
a: Discretionary: manager decides every trade (most common)
Non-discretionary: manager recommends; client approves each trade
Advisory: manager only advises; client executes

cards.q: What changed for PMS benchmarking from April 2023?
a: Every PMS investment approach is grouped into one of four strategies (equity, debt, hybrid, multi-asset) and compared against a common benchmark, with data published through APMI.

cards.q: Minimum ticket: MF vs PMS vs AIF?
a: MF: as low as a few hundred rupees. PMS: ₹50 lakh. AIF: typically ₹1 crore.

cards.q: Ownership: MF vs PMS?
a: MF: units of a pooled fund. PMS: the securities themselves, in the client's own demat account.

cards.q: How is PMS taxed differently from a mutual fund?
a: Every sale by the manager is a taxable event in the client's own hands. In an MF, tax arises at fund level and the investor is taxed only on redemption.

cards.q: PMS fees vs MF fees?
a: PMS: fixed and/or performance fee, set by agreement. MF: expense ratio capped by SEBI. AIF: management fee plus carry.

cards.q: What certification does a PMS distributor need?
a: NISM Series XXI-A (PMS Distributors).

cards.q: What is an APRN, and why does 31 July 2025 matter?
a: APMI Registration Number. Since 31 July 2025, distributors without an APRN cannot bring in new PMS business or receive commission.

cards.q: Who needs an EUIN in PMS distribution?
a: Employees of non-individual distributors.

cards.q: How is a PMS distributor paid?
a: Trail commission only. Upfront commissions and upfront fees to clients are not permitted.

cards.q: What option does every PMS client always have?
a: Direct onboarding with the portfolio manager, with no distributor. So our value (selection, monitoring, service) must be clear.

cards.q: Client A: ₹3 Cr invested, PMS is a 17% slice on top of a solid core. Client B: ₹55 L total savings, wants ₹50 L in PMS. Verdict?
a: Client A is suitable. Client B is eligible but a red flag: 91% of everything, no core and no emergency buffer. Mutual funds first, PMS later.

cards.q: Suitability check 1: investible surplus?
a: Suitable if ₹50 lakh is a slice of a larger portfolio. Red flag if it is most of the client's investible wealth.

cards.q: Suitability check 2: existing core?
a: Suitable if the client already has diversified MFs, debt and an emergency fund. Red flag if PMS would be their first equity.

cards.q: Suitability check 3: horizon?
a: Suitable if 3–5+ years without needing the money. Red flag if they may need it within 2–3 years.

cards.q: Suitability check 4: drawdown tolerance?
a: Suitable if they have stayed invested through a 30%+ fall before. Red flag if they have never seen a real fall, or sold in one.

cards.q: Suitability checks 5 and 6: tax awareness and engagement?
a: Tax: understands each trade creates a tax event (red flag: expects MF-like deferral). Engagement: comfortable with monthly statements and full trade lists (red flag: wants hands-off and simple).

cards.q: The 5 PMS discovery questions?
a: What share of your total investments would this ₹50 L be?
What did you do with your equity in March 2020?
If this fell 30% while the Nifty fell 15%, how would you react?
Do you need any of this money in the next 3 years?
Any stocks or sectors to exclude (e.g. employer shares)?

cards.q: Why does a PMS behave so differently from the index?
a: The Nifty 50 spreads money across 50 stocks; a typical PMS holds about 20, so each stock carries far more weight. The same concentration that creates the upside creates the downside.

cards.q: The due-diligence areas to check before recommending a strategy?
a: Track record (after-fee, 3/5/7 yrs, incl. 2020 & 2022)
Manager & team · Process & style consistency
Portfolio concentration · Risk (worst fall, recovery)
Costs · Disclosure Document & agreement
Compare 2–3 strategies on APMI data

cards.q: What does "track record" due diligence look at?
a: After-fee returns vs benchmark over 3, 5 and 7 years, including how the strategy did in falls such as 2020 and 2022.

cards.q: What does "portfolio" due diligence look at?
a: Number of stocks, top-10 weight, sector and market-cap concentration, and cash calls.

cards.q: What are the three PMS fee structures?
a: Fixed: a flat % of assets a year
Performance-linked: share of profits above a hurdle, usually with a high-water mark
Hybrid: lower fixed fee plus a profit share

cards.q: What is the cap on PMS operating expenses?
a: 0.5% a year, excluding brokerage.

cards.q: Fee example, ₹1 Cr, +18% year: A = 2.5% fixed; B = 1% + 20% above a 10% hurdle?
a: A: fee ₹2.5 L → net gain ₹15.5 L. B: ₹1 L + 20% of ₹8 L = ₹2.6 L → net gain ₹15.4 L. Almost the same. (Hypothetical, before GST, brokerage and expenses.)

cards.q: Same fee options in a −10% year (₹10 L loss)?
a: A: still ₹2.5 L fee → net loss ₹12.5 L. B: only the ₹1 L fixed fee → net loss ₹11 L. Show the client both years before choosing.

cards.q: What is a high-water mark?
a: Profit share is charged only on gains above the portfolio's previous peak, so the client does not pay twice for recovering the same ground.

cards.q: High-water mark example: ₹1 Cr → ₹1.20 Cr → ₹1 Cr → ₹1.15 Cr → ₹1.35 Cr. Where is profit share charged?
a: Year 1 (new peak of ₹1.20 Cr). None in years 2–3 (regaining lost ground). Year 4 only on the ₹15 L above the old ₹1.20 Cr peak.

cards.q: The PMS onboarding checklist?
a: Suitability documented and signed
Disclosure Document shared; risks explained
Agreement, fee schedule, exit load reviewed
Fee illustration in rupees: up, flat, down years
Direct option mentioned; our role explained
KYC, demat, bank in client's name
DDPI / POA scope explained · Nominee added
APRN & EUIN on documents; trail disclosed

cards.q: How is a PMS judged?
a: On at least 3 years of after-fee returns against its benchmark, never on one quarter or on the strategy's headline number.

cards.q: The PMS review rhythm?
a: Monthly: statement; check unusual trades, cash, drawdowns
Quarterly: call/note on performance vs benchmark, changes, manager commentary
Annually: full review with the client

cards.q: The annual review agenda?
a: Client update · Returns (own account, after fees)
Risk (largest fall vs benchmark)
Portfolio (concentration, turnover, drift, cash)
Manager changes · Costs in ₹ and tax
Fit as a share of total portfolio
Decision: stay, top up, reduce or exit, with reasons

cards.q: "Factsheet says 40%, why have I only made 12%?"
a: Entry timing. Client A joined at launch (100 → 140, up 40%); Client B joined at 125 after a strong run (up 12%). Show the client's own after-fee account return vs benchmark for the same period.

cards.q: Lagging benchmark for 1 year, process unchanged, style out of favour?
a: Stay, and explain the style cycle.

cards.q: Lagging benchmark AND peers for 3+ years?
a: Review for exit.

cards.q: The fund manager or key team leaves?
a: Review immediately. Proactively inform the client; no panic and no automatic exit.

cards.q: Style drift away from what was sold?
a: Review. It is no longer the product the client bought.

cards.q: What must be set out before any PMS exit?
a: The exit load, the tax on gains, and the cost of rebuilding elsewhere.

cards.q: Why is the emotional test harder in PMS than in MFs?
a: Bigger swings from 15–30 stocks
Full visibility: every red stock in their own demat
Switching costs real tax and exit load
Peer talk about "last year's top PMS"

cards.q: The 6-step playbook for a sharp fall or long underperformance?
a: Set expectations at onboarding (show worst past fall)
Call before they call, newest clients first
Separate the market from the manager
Check the process, not the price
Show the cost of leaving (tax, exit load, selling low)
Record and follow up in writing

cards.q: "This stock is down 40%, tell the manager to sell it." Bias and response?
a: Loss aversion and illusion of control. "You're paying the manager for the whole portfolio. Let's judge the portfolio against its benchmark, not one stock."

cards.q: "My friend's PMS made 60% last year. Let's move." Bias and response?
a: Recency and herd. "Let's compare both on after-fee returns over five years, including their worst year."

cards.q: "The market is up but my PMS isn't." Bias and response?
a: Short-term framing. "This style lags in some phases. Here's how it did across a full cycle."

cards.q: Talk-track when a dip is within what was discussed at onboarding?
a: "This dip is within what we discussed at the start. Exiting now would lock in both the loss and the tax."

cards.q: Why can a client's return differ from the published strategy return?
a: Each portfolio is built at a different time and price, with different cash flows. Ask for your own account's after-fee return.

cards.q: What hidden costs sit beyond the headline fee?
a: Brokerage, custody and demat charges, and GST on fees and profit share. Ask for the all-in cost.

cards.q: How does manager turnover affect the client's tax?
a: Every sale is a capital gains event for the client, so high turnover can mean a bigger tax bill. Tax on PMS fees is not straightforward; involve the client's CA.

cards.q: What are the SEBI caps on PMS exit loads?
a: Up to 3% in year 1, 2% in year 2 and 1% in year 3. The actual load is set in each agreement.

cards.q: What is an in-specie transfer?
a: Many providers accept existing shares instead of cash, and can return securities instead of selling on exit. Check the provider's policy.

cards.q: Why does the DDPI / POA scope matter?
a: The authority signed over the demat and bank account defines what the manager can do. Read what you authorise before signing.

cards.q: Nomination and corporate actions in a PMS?
a: Nominee, dividends, bonuses and voting rights all sit in the client's own demat. Add a nominee to the PMS demat too.

cards.q: What to ask about high-water marks and cash flows?
a: Whether and when the high-water mark resets, and whether fees are charged on contributions or withdrawals.

cards.q: Top-ups and partial withdrawals?
a: Rules on minimum top-ups and partial withdrawals vary by provider and agreement. Know them before the money is needed.

cards.q: What must be in place before dealing with PMS clients?
a: NISM XXI-A certification and a valid APRN (plus EUIN for employees of non-individual distributors).

cards.q: How must PMS performance be shown?
a: Net of fees, against the benchmark and peers. Never quote headline or pre-fee returns, or cherry-pick periods or strategies.

cards.q: The PMS complaint escalation path?
a: Provider → SEBI SCORES → Smart ODR.

cards.q: Key PMS compliance don'ts?
a: Source PMS business without an APRN
Treat ₹50 L as proof of suitability
Take or imply upfront commission or fees
Recommend switches for commission
Promise returns or recovery timelines

questions.q: What is the SEBI minimum investment for a PMS?
o: ₹10 lakh
₹25 lakh
₹50 lakh
₹1 crore
questions.why: PMS needs ₹50 lakh. AIFs typically need ₹1 crore.

questions.q: Where are the securities in a PMS held?
o: In the client's own demat account
In the AMC's pooled fund
In the distributor's demat account
With the RTA
questions.why: The client owns the shares directly and can see every holding and trade.

questions.q: In which type of PMS does the manager decide every trade?
o: Non-discretionary
Advisory
Execution-only
Discretionary
questions.why: Discretionary is the most common type. In non-discretionary the client approves each trade; in advisory the manager only advises.

questions.q: What does a PMS distributor need before dealing with PMS clients?
o: Only an ARN from AMFI
NISM Series XXI-A and an APRN from APMI
SEBI RIA registration
NISM Series V-A only
questions.why: Employees of non-individual distributors also need an EUIN. Since 31 July 2025, no APRN means no new business or commission.

questions.q: How is a PMS distributor paid?
o: Upfront commission on each new client
Trail commission only
An upfront fee charged to the client
A share of the manager's profit fee
questions.why: Upfront commissions and upfront fees to clients are not permitted.

questions.q: A client has exactly ₹55 lakh in total savings and wants ₹50 lakh in PMS. What is correct?
o: Suitable, because the ₹50 lakh minimum is met
Suitable if the strategy has strong past returns
Invest the full ₹55 lakh to qualify for lower fees
Eligible but not suitable; suggest MFs first, PMS later
questions.why: Eligible is not suitable. That is 91% of their savings, with no core portfolio and no emergency buffer.

questions.q: Which client profile is a red flag for PMS?
o: PMS would be the client's first equity investment
Client has a diversified MF and debt core
Client stayed invested through a 30% fall
Client has a 5+ year horizon
questions.why: PMS should sit on top of a solid core portfolio, never replace it.

questions.q: What is the minimum horizon for a suitable PMS client?
o: 6 months
1 year
3–5+ years without needing the money
Until the next market rally
questions.why: If the client may need the money within 2–3 years, it is a red flag.

questions.q: Which discovery question best tests drawdown tolerance?
o: "What is your PAN number?"
"Which PMS did your friend invest in?"
"Do you prefer large-cap stocks?"
"What did you do with your equity investments in March 2020?"
questions.why: Past behaviour in a real fall reveals tolerance. Also ask how they'd react to a 30% fall while the Nifty fell 15%.

questions.q: A client expects PMS to defer tax like a mutual fund. What should you explain?
o: PMS is tax-free for ₹50 lakh+ investors
Every trade by the manager is a tax event in the client's hands
Tax is paid only on final exit
The PMS provider pays the tax
questions.why: Expecting MF-like deferral is a suitability red flag. High turnover can mean a bigger tax bill.

questions.q: Which is the most important track-record check in PMS due diligence?
o: Best single-quarter return
Headline pre-fee return since launch
After-fee returns vs benchmark over 3, 5 and 7 years, including falls
Number of clients the PMS has
questions.why: Include how the strategy did in falls such as 2020 and 2022.

questions.q: Name the three PMS fee structures.
o: Fixed, performance-linked and hybrid
Entry load, exit load and expense ratio
Upfront, trail and carry
Management, custody and stamp duty
questions.why: Fixed is a flat %; performance-linked is a profit share above a hurdle; hybrid is a lower fixed fee plus a profit share.

questions.q: ₹1 Cr portfolio falls 10%. Option A: 2.5% fixed. Option B: 1% fixed + 20% above a 10% hurdle. Net loss under each?
o: A: ₹12.5 lakh; B: ₹11 lakh
A: ₹11 lakh; B: ₹12.5 lakh
Both ₹10 lakh
A: ₹12.5 lakh; B: ₹13 lakh
questions.why: In a down year A still charges ₹2.5 L, while B charges only its ₹1 L fixed fee (hypothetical, before GST and expenses).

questions.q: What is a high-water mark?
o: The highest NAV the strategy has ever reached
A cap on the manager's fixed fee
Profit share is charged only on gains above the portfolio's previous peak
The minimum return the manager guarantees
questions.why: It stops the client paying twice for recovering the same ground.

questions.q: What is the cap on PMS operating expenses (excluding brokerage)?
o: 1% a year
0.5% a year
2.5% a year
There is no cap
questions.why: Operating expenses, excluding brokerage, are capped at 0.5% a year.

questions.q: On what basis should a PMS be judged?
o: The last quarter's return
The strategy's headline factsheet number
Returns compared with a bank FD
3+ years of after-fee returns vs its benchmark
questions.why: Never judge a PMS on one quarter or on the headline strategy number.

questions.q: Factsheet shows +40%, but the client has made only 12%. Most likely reason?
o: The manager charged the client a hidden fee
Different entry timing, prices and cash flows
The factsheet is wrong
The client's stocks are different by mistake
questions.why: Each account is built at a different time and price. Show the client their own after-fee account return.

questions.q: A PMS lagged its benchmark for 1 year; process unchanged, style out of favour. Action?
o: Stay, and explain the style cycle
Exit immediately
Switch to last year's top PMS
Stop the monthly statements
questions.why: Review for exit only after 3+ years behind benchmark AND peers.

questions.q: The star fund manager has just left the PMS firm. What should you do?
o: Exit all clients automatically
Wait three years before reviewing
Say nothing unless the client asks
Review immediately and inform the client proactively
questions.why: No panic and no automatic exit, but an immediate review.

questions.q: Before recommending any PMS exit, what must you set out?
o: Only the last month's return
The manager's personal track record
Exit load, tax on gains and the cost of rebuilding elsewhere
The new PMS's marketing brochure
questions.why: Exiting has real costs in a PMS, because tax falls in the client's own hands.

questions.q: Why is the emotional test sharper in PMS than in mutual funds?
o: PMS has lower returns than MFs
PMS clients cannot see their holdings
Concentrated swings, full visibility of every stock, and real switching costs
PMS portfolios hold more stocks than MFs
questions.why: Wealthy clients also hear about "last year's top PMS" at every gathering.

questions.q: "This stock is down 40%, tell the manager to sell it." Which bias?
o: Anchoring
Home bias
Overconfidence in the index
Loss aversion and illusion of control
questions.why: Respond: you pay the manager for the whole portfolio; judge it against its benchmark, not one stock.

questions.q: "My friend's PMS made 60% last year. Let's move." Best response?
o: Switch immediately to capture the gains
Compare both on after-fee returns over 5 years, including their worst year
Tell the client their friend is lying
Promise the current PMS will do better next year
questions.why: This is recency and herd behaviour.

questions.q: The portfolio is down 28% while the Nifty is down 12%. What is a key step before advising?
o: Separate the market from the manager and check the process
Exit today to stop further losses
Move everything to the friend's PMS
Ignore the client until markets recover
questions.why: If the manager, process and portfolio quality are intact, the case for staying holds. Record the conversation.

questions.q: When should a client first see the strategy's worst historical fall?
o: Only after a fall happens
At the 3-year review
Never; it may scare the client
At onboarding, before investing
questions.why: Setting expectations at onboarding is step one of the playbook.

questions.q: What are the SEBI caps on PMS exit loads?
o: Up to 3% in year 1, 2% in year 2 and 1% in year 3
1% flat for the first year only
No exit load is allowed in PMS
Up to 5% in every year
questions.why: The actual load is set in each agreement, within these caps.

questions.q: Which is a "hidden cost" beyond the headline PMS fee?
o: Stamp duty on MF units
The ELSS lock-in
GST on fees and profit share, brokerage, custody and demat charges
The NISM exam fee
questions.why: Ask for the all-in cost, not just the management fee.

questions.q: A client wants to fund a PMS with shares they already own. What is true?
o: It is never allowed; only cash is accepted
Many providers accept an in-specie transfer; check the provider's policy
The shares must be sold first by the distributor
Only mutual fund units can be transferred
questions.why: Many providers can also return securities instead of selling on exit.

questions.q: Which of these is a compliance DON'T?
o: Treating the ₹50 lakh minimum as proof of suitability
Mentioning the direct onboarding option
Showing performance net of fees vs benchmark
Recording reasons for every recommendation
questions.why: Also don't source business without an APRN, quote pre-fee returns, or take upfront commission.

questions.q: What is the PMS complaint escalation path?
o: AMFI, then NISM
Provider, then SEBI SCORES, then Smart ODR
Only the distributor's branch
The stock exchange helpline only
